title: Investigation of whether a drug, Anakinra, will help people with severe lung failure called acute respiratory distress syndrome
official: A Phase II randomised clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy of anakinra in patients with the acute respiratory distress syndrome (AnakARDS)
summary:
Background and study aims 
Severe lung failure, called acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), is a common problem for patients admitted to the intensive care unit. Most of these patients need help from a breathing machine, and many suffer longer term ill health or die. Other organs, like the kidneys, can also stop working properly. Currently, there are no effective drug treatments for lung failure. The immune response, called inflammation, is a natural process. Parts of the blood (proteins and cells) increase in number to help the body fight harmful conditions, like infection. However, for some patients, inflammation goes into overdrive which can lead to damage to the lungs and other organs.
Anakinra is a medicine that helps reduce inflammation and is safely used to treat arthritis (painful joints caused by too much inflammation). It has also been studied in people with COVID-19. In those with high levels of the protein suPAR, anakinra helped more patients survive. Since COVID-19 and lung failure are similar, we believe anakinra could help people with lung failure, especially those with high suPAR levels.

Who can participate? 
Patients aged 16 years and over with lung failure

What does the study involve? 
The participants are randomly allocated into two groups so that half will receive anakinra combined with usual care while the other half will receive usual care only. Patients being treated with anakinra will receive 200 mg, intravenous (into a vein), 8-hourly, for up to 10 days. Researchers will assess whether anakinra improves organ function and survival, and whether patients with higher suPAR levels benefit more. This may help identify those most likely to respond to this treatment in the future.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Participants may or may not benefit directly from taking part in this study. Instead, their participation will give us information to help us treat other patients with severe lung failure in the future.
Although this study drug is already in common use for other conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and has been widely studied for patients with severe lung failure during the COVID-19 pandemic, it is possible participants will experience unwanted or unexpected side effects related to the medication. As this is an immunomodulatory drug the most likely side effects include infection, low blood counts, liver test abnormalities and skin reactions. As the drug will be administered intravenously for this study skin reactions are less likely. Participants will be monitored closely through daily general observations and blood testing to observe for infection, blood counts and liver function. As the participants are critically ill within the ICU setting, they will be closely monitored and clinical response to any deterioration is rapid. The study drug is primarily eliminated in the kidneys and clearance reduced with decreased renal function. Patients with severe renal injury or those who are receiving haemodialysis will receive a reduced dose of 100 mg.

Where is the study run from? 
Belfast Health and Social Care Trust (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
December 2026 to November 2030

Who is funding the study? 
National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Efficacy and Mechanism – Advanced Fellowship Programme (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Andrew Boyle, Andrew.boyle@qub.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Adults (aged 16 years or older)
2. Within the first 48 hours of meeting ARDS criteria as defined by fulfilling each of the following: 
2.1. Receiving respiratory support via either:
2.1.1. Invasive mechanical ventilation (with minimum positive end-expiratory pressure 5 cm H2O)
2.1.2. Non-invasive ventilation (including continuous positive airway pressure) (with minimum end-expiratory pressure 5 cm H2O), or
2.1.3. High-flow nasal oxygen (≥30 l/min)
2.2. With a known acute clinical insult, or new, or worsening respiratory dysfunction, and  
2.3. Bilateral infiltrates on lung imaging not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse/atelectasis, or nodules, and 
2.4. Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload, and
2.5. Ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen to fraction of inspired oxygen (PF ratio) <40 kPa from arterial blood

Criteria 2.3 to 2.5 must be within the same 24-hour time-period. The time of onset of ARDS is when the last criterion is met.
Exclusion criteria:
1. Planned withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment within the next 24 hours 
2. Confirmed diagnosis for coronavirus disease (COVID-19)
3. Known hypersensitivity to active substance or any excipient listed in section 6.1 of the SmPC
4. Known hypersensitivity to E. coli-derived proteins
5. Concurrent or recent (in past 4 weeks) treatment with anakinra
6. Severe liver disease (Child-Pugh C)
7. Patients with confirmed pregnancy or lactating
8. Patients previously enrolled within the trial
9. Patients receiving active or ongoing treatment for malignancy
10. Known active tuberculosis infection or, if known, latent TB treated for less than 4 weeks with appropriate anti-tuberculosis therapy per local guidelines
11.	Receiving immunosuppression as part of a pre- or post-organ transplant treatment plan
12.	Neutropenia (defined as an absolute neutrophil count <1.5 x 10e9/L)
13.	Known Hepatitis B virus or Hepatitis C virus
14. Any other medical condition or treatment that, at the clinical discretion of the investigator, is considered not in the participants best interest to start treatment with the IMP based on the approved version of the IMP SmPC
15.	Patient has a known body weight <50 kg
16. Declined consent
